[...] Pitch accent in the Apachean languages, though superficially similar to that of Chinese in that each word has a definite pitch melody, actually belongs to the third type distinguished above, the pitch accent of the Apachean word being the sum of the tonemes of its constituent syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Lipan, like the other Apachean languages, is a syllable-tone language (high, low, falling, rising tonemes; contour tones only on long vowels/vowel clusters); syllables are evenly stressed and there is no distinctive word-, phrase- or sentence-level accentual pattern beyond the sequence of syllable tones, i.e. no contrastive or positionally fixed word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the source denies any accentual pattern above the syllable tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Hoijer notes speakers vary 'accentual patterns.. in response to emotional and other non-linguistic factors' but calls these 'individual and haphazard'; 'minor differences' among the six languages' accentual systems are explicitly set aside. Illustrative forms are Navajo unless otherwise stated (fn. 3).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the utterance/word generally (connected speech), not citation forms specifically; it is a blanket statement for all six Apachean languages, Lipan named explicitly, based on Hoijer's own Lipan fieldwork (1938, per Hoijer 1945: 193 and Webster 2007: 105).
new_statements.identity_note: Hoijer 1943 is a pan-Apachean statement that explicitly names Lipan (lipa1241) among the six languages covered and rests on Hoijer's own 1938 Lipan fieldwork at Mescalero, NM (chief consultant Augustina Zuazua); illustrative forms in the article are Navajo. No Lipan-only phonological description could be opened; the language has had no fluent speakers since mid-20th c. (Hoijer 1975: 5, quoted in Webster 2007), so all descriptions derive from Hoijer/Gatschet/Goddard records.

sources.note: p.38: explicitly lists Lipan among the six Apachean languages to which the remarks 'apply with equal force'; an Apachean utterance 'is a succession of evenly stressed syllables each of which possesses a clearly defined pitch accent or tone'; 'there are no distinctive accentual patterns characteristic of the word, the phrase, or the sentence'. Four syllable tonemes (high, low, falling, rising). Examples are Navajo unless stated.

Gives 30 consonants, 16 vowels, four tones (high, low, falling, rising; contour tones only on long vowels), uncited; nothing on stress. Bibliography used to build the source list (Hoijer 1938/1942/1943-46/1975, Gatschet mss, Goddard ms, Opler 2001 HNAI, Webster 1999).
